title: Step 1: Architecture and request lifecycle; contract-first API with OpenAPI
summary: TraceLite is one Go server, one PostgreSQL database and one React app, with openapi.yaml as the contract between them. A request goes browser, Vite proxy, ServeMux, handler, service, store, pgx, PostgreSQL and back; names change form at two well-defined places.

examples.title: One request through every layer, printed hop by hop

annotations.note: The wire type, abridged. Its json tags are where snake_case columns become camelCase members; nothing else in the request path renames anything.
A fixed id and a timestamp written in Istanbul time (+03), so the output is the same on every run. Step 2 has the real schema.
Go 1.22 patterns: the method and a named wildcard in the pattern itself. r.Pattern (Go 1.23) reports which pattern matched, which is also what TraceLite's request log records.
The id is parsed before any SQL runs, and travels to PostgreSQL as a parameter: the extended protocol sends the statement and the value separately.

r.Context() is passed down to pgx. If the browser goes away, the request's context is canceled and the call returns at once: by default pgx sets a deadline on the connection and closes it. Sending PostgreSQL a real cancel request is opt-in, through pgconn's CancelRequestContextWatcherHandler.

The error leg: an id that doesn't parse, or parses but names nothing (pgx.ErrNoRows), takes the same route and gets an RFC 9457 problem instead of a resource. Step 4 maps every error this way, in one function.
pgx returns timestamptz in the process's local zone ("Local"). The wire carries UTC with Z (06:30Z for 09:30+03), whatever zone the server runs in.

What vite.config.ts's server.proxy does: requests under /api go to the Go server; everything else, the app itself, Vite serves. The browser only ever talks to vite.URL, so the page and the API share one origin and the browser never sends a CORS preflight.

examples.title: The spec as the yardstick: checking a Go wire type against openapi.yaml

annotations.note: The Requirement schema from the spec below, reduced to what this check reads. The spec, not the Go struct and not the table, defines what a client receives.
The check runs on the encoded bytes, exactly what a handler would write, so struct tags, omitempty and custom marshalers are all part of what is checked.

Three kinds of drift: a required member missing, a member the spec doesn't know, and a value outside the enum. Step 14 turns this into a test; a production suite would load openapi.yaml into a JSON Schema validator, which also checks types, patterns and lengths. The idea is the same.
Each edit compiles, passes go vet and looks fine in a diff. Both change the wire, and neither changes the TypeScript client, which keeps reading parentId and description.
A struct conversion: the field names and types match, and since Go 1.8 tags are ignored when converting, so the same values are encoded both ways.
The third kind of drift is in the data, not the type: a display label in a field the spec defines as an enum of lowercase values.

use_cases: Starting a full-stack feature: write the operation and schemas into openapi.yaml first, then the migration, the store query, the handler and the client
Reviewing a change: a diff to openapi.yaml is a change to the contract and needs both sides
Debugging: following a request through the proxy, router, handler, store and database, one layer at a time
Local development with one origin: Vite proxies /api, so cookies, relative URLs and fetch work without CORS
strengths: The contract is a reviewed file in the repo, not whatever the Go structs happen to encode; TypeScript types are generated from it
One origin in development (Vite proxy) and production (the Go binary serves the app), so there is no CORS configuration to drift between them
Every layer has one job and one package; a bug report names a layer: decoding, rules, SQL, or rendering
Names change form in exactly two places, Go struct tags (SQL to Go to JSON) and nowhere in TypeScript, because the client uses the wire names directly
weaknesses: The Go wire types are written by hand next to the spec; only a test notices when they drift
Contract-first means writing YAML before code, which feels slow for a one-person project until the first client and server disagree
Three representations of a requirement (row, Go model, wire JSON) mean mapping code in the store and the handler
The Vite proxy hides cross-origin problems in development that a deployment on two origins would have

pitfalls.title: Letting the Go structs become the contract
pitfalls.detail: If the spec is updated from the code after the fact, a tag edit silently changes the API. Change openapi.yaml first, then the Go type, and let the contract test compare them.

pitfalls.title: Calling the Go server directly from the browser in development
pitfalls.detail: fetch("http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/...") from a page on :5173 is cross-origin and needs CORS headers that production never sends. Use relative URLs and the Vite proxy.
pitfalls.good: fetch("/api/requirements/" + id) // same origin; Vite forwards /api

pitfalls.title: snake_case leaking onto the wire
pitfalls.detail: A tag copied from the column name (json:"parent_id") breaks every client that reads parentId. Wire names are camelCase, always written as explicit tags.

pitfalls.title: Dropping the request context
pitfalls.detail: context.Background() in a handler's query keeps the handler waiting for a result after the client disconnected, holding a pooled connection. Pass r.Context() all the way to pgx.

quiz.q: In development, the browser loads the app from :5173 and calls /api/requirements/{id}. Who answers?
options: The Go server, through Vite's proxy, on the same origin
The Go server directly, with CORS headers
quiz.why: server.proxy forwards /api to the Go server; the browser only ever talks to the dev server's origin.

options: In the json tag of the Go wire type
quiz.why: SQL keeps snake_case, sqlc maps columns to Go field names, and the wire type's json tags produce camelCase; the client uses the wire names unchanged.

quiz.q: Which file is the source of truth for the JSON a client receives?
quiz.why: Contract-first: the spec is written first and both sides conform to it. TypeScript types are generated from it; the Go types are checked against it.

quiz.q: A handler adds omitempty to description. What does example 2 report?
options: Nothing: the field still exists in Go
missing description, when the description is empty
quiz.why: omitempty drops the member when it is empty; the spec lists description as required.
